utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we start the cross-examination, are there any procedural matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. President, Your Honours, in light of the developments today -- I should say yesterday and today, and last week as well, it would seem to us - and I'm making a joint motion at this moment on behalf of both Mr. Blagojevic's Defence team and Mr. Jokic's Defence team - it would seem the most prudent thing at this point would be to ask that we not go forward with the cross-examination of Mr. Ruez at this point until we've had an opportunity to review the statements that will be generated from both Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic. It's our understanding that the Prosecution, sometime in the next two or three weeks, will begin to question these two gentlemen. Obviously this impacts our case tremendously. We do believe that a one-month continuance, irrespective of whether we go forward with Mr. Ruez's cross-examination or not, will be necessary. And let me explain why. All right? I notice that I piqued your interest, Mr. President. I anticipated that sort of reaction. Frankly, I would ask -- I would like to have more, more time, but I think a month is reasonable. And here is the reason: One, it will -- from what I understand, it will take the Prosecution one or two weeks to debrief these two gentlemen, perhaps even longer. They haven't even begun the process yet, even though, for instance, with Mr. Nikolic, the plea was negotiated last week or the week before but they have yet to begin that process, in part because the gentleman that are most familiar with the case and are going to be part of the debriefing process are here. And so obviously while they're here, they may not be able to get to that. Because frankly, it would seem to me, they should have by now had these statements. Secondly, the statements will need to be translated so that we can have them and our clients can have them and review them. We will need to also view the statement very carefully to see what investigation we might need to do, and we might need to do some immediate investigation before we can resume. It must be kept in mind that under the new payment system with the Registrar - and I hate to talk about money and resources, but it's a reality in this case - we have very limited resources at this trial stage for investigative purposes. With these two new developments, Your Honour, it really stretches us to the limit of, one, being able to go forward with the trial and at the same time investigate. And I might say, at least with respect to Mr. Blagojevic, Mr. Nikolic is perhaps the most critical witness for the Prosecution at this moment. And I might be overstating it, and I'm sure if I am, Mr. McCloskey, who has just taken the front seat and is the lead counsel, will be more than happy to correct me. Also in Mr. Obrenovic's negotiated statement, whatever -- you know, the one that was accepted today, it's also -- that also impacts Mr. Blagojevic's case. I don't want to speak on behalf of Mr. Jokic, but clearly it seems to me that it highly impacts the Jokic Defence team. So in light of all these matters, we think that a one-month continuance is not reasonable. You know, we have limited resources, we have to go to the scenes. And what I fear - what I fear - my greatest fear is the Prosecution indicated to us in a letter, which we gave in our motion because I asked for their handwritten notes -- they told us that they're going to give us three weeks before they put these gentleman on to testify. Three weeks is not enough, Your Honour, to prepare, not when they've had seven years to prepare this case. They have the resources. They have an armada of lawyers, investigators, parallels that are out there, you know, night and day, and here I am with my little team. You know, plus one person out in the field. Not the same, Your Honour. The other thing is if, for instance - and I can just see this now happening - they put them on at the end of July. There is the Prosecution sunning, basking in the Mediterranean Sea, you know, relaxing, as they should, when we're going to be out in the field trying to track down witnesses when everybody knows, at least in Europe, August is the month for vacation. And I'm not talking about personally my going on vacation but trying to track down witnesses during the three-week session is clearly not -- not fair and equitable, not when we have these limited resources. So we would like to at least front load as much as we can so that I don't have to come back and say, "Your Honour, I need more time." I think one month is reasonable. I don't know what the Prosecution's position is. I certainly want to give them enough time so they can milk all they want the witnesses that they have right now, the two gentleman, Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic. And I'm sure that they're going to want to debrief them, you know, over and over and over again, because, you know, they have a lot of information that they -- and I'm sure that they want to double-check that information, because they're going to be making some sentencing remarks at the conclusion of their testimony. So I think on behalf of both Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic, one, I would be asking today that we continue the cross-examination of Mr. Ruez; and number two, and more importantly, I'm going to underscore this - so if I can get only one of the two wishes, I would like the latter, which is the one-month continuance. Because clearly we're talking about trying to -- to be adequately prepared for trial. And when you think about the Statute, it guarantees equality of arms. Clearly there's never going to be equality of arms even in a perfect world. However time does permit us to at least having a fighting chance of being properly prepared and making sure that Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic get a very fair trial, which I am sure is the ultimate goal of this -- of this Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as counsel for Mr. Jokic, the accused, I would just like to put forward the following remarks: There is no need to repeat the fact that over the last 10 or 15 days many vital things have happened which clearly affect the position of both the Prosecution and the Defence in this case. You are well aware of the fact that only last night we received the statement of facts in B/C/S, as well as the plea agreement between the Prosecution and Dragan Obrenovic. You also know that the plea agreement that was the subject of our discussion today, the plea agreement and the guilty plea, three counts of the indictment have been amended that directly concern our client, Dragan Jokic; 46.10, 46.11, and 46.12 of the amended indictment. True enough. We as the Defence team, perhaps due partly to difficult concerning the transcript and interpretation, we have concepts such as control and now the superior -- which is changed into the superior position or superiority, superior command of Dragan Obrenovic. This very much changes the whole thing for us, and the question we're asking ourselves now is: How essential this change to the indictment and how does it concern Dragan Jokic? It is deemed to be essential. It is in the view of that -- in view of that and in view of the arguments put forth by Mr. Karnavas, asking on behalf of both Defence teams for a period of time to be given to us to work through the statements and study the facts, given therein, as well as to discuss these with our client and in view of the amended indictment, we do believe, Your Honours, that it would be fair and in the best interest of justice, in the best interest of the Defence, not to cross-examine Mr. Ruez until we are granted time to do what I have said. I am not saying all of this to in any way obstruct this case. I do not want to bring my team into a situation where we would be putting things off and delaying the case with no need. I'm only saying this because we may well have a situation where we would omit to ask Mr. Ruez about some vital facts concerning this case, facts which might affect the further course of our case. If you accept these arguments and allow us a period of time to prepare all that I've talked about, which we believe a month would be a fair amount of time to be granted, I would ask you therefore to put off the continuation of Mr. Ruez's cross-examination and not to start today. As we've studied today the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as concerns the indictment, I thought that maybe we should pass the floor to my co-counsel, Ms. Sinatra, who will point out the legal framework and the relevant facts, the relevant legal facts which support our proposal, our motion. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that both counsel Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Karnavas have well-argued our points. I just wanted to make sure -- and I know the Court is familiar with -- to continue right now with an indictment that is not going to be the final indictment, with continued amendments and fundamental changes in the allegations against the client, the accused here, would be fundamental error at this point and would violate Article 20 and 21 of the Statute. But also, the Prosecution, although they are alleging that they're putting forth this amended indictment, they have not followed the procedures involved with amending the indictment. They have not requested leave of court. Under Rule 73, once we have this proposal before us, then we should have 30 days to respond and object to any amendments to the indictment. I know that recently that period of time was shortened by the Trial Chamber ten days, but now that's renewed because we have new proposals that drastically change the indictment. Now, the other proposals for the amendment of the indictment -- I mean, they might have said they were erratas. But these new amendments to the indictment affect dramatically the allegations and charges against Mr. Jokic. We ask that this Court grant a continuance. We cannot go forward with any cross-examination of Mr. Ruez. And we ask that you stay these proceedings for a minimum of 30 days and allow us an additional amount of time to respond and object to the proposed amendments to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you mean that we'll have this witness unfinished under the oath for another month, then he comes back, you cross-examine this witness? I am right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because if we were forced to cross-examine him even at this time and we were able to analyse the changes in the indictment, we would have to re-call him anyway, possibly, for further questioning. So it would -- first of all, I believe it's fundamental error to proceed in the trial, whether it's questioning of a witness or whether it's, you know, another meeting in court to raise issues, until we have a final indictment. But we would in all likelihood need to re-call Mr. Ruez after the final analysis of this -- these proposed amendments anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us hear the motive of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I recall, there's one difference: Mr. Karnavas would prefer to go on with the cross, and Ms. Sinatra and Mr. Stojanovic prefer to stop the cross. That's my understanding. I can agree with them in the sense that there are some small changes in the indictment now. Those changes are clearly outlined in both plea agreements. We will be filing a changed indictment upon the Court's order to do so, and I think the Court has indicated justifiably so that it will give counsel time to respond, as I think they should have. How this affects the questioning of Mr. Ruez and the link between the two issues, I have not understood from their argument. Mr. Ruez is mainly on direct was meant to be talking about crime scenes. He did interview the accused, and maybe they will take him to areas beyond the scope of direct. But any concern they have regarding Mr. Ruez and their ability to cross-examine him, I believe can be solved by bringing Mr. Ruez back and -- which I think we can do. Regarding the length of the continuance, I leave that to your discretion. I would point out to you that Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic are certainly not the foundational witnesses of the Prosecution's case. They are co-accused, and as such I will be offering you my view on how much credibility to give them. This case will be based on the witnesses and evidence before you and any weight or value of those witnesses should be based on the evidence as a whole. The process by which the statements you see in the plea agreements was a lengthy and a detailed process with Defence counsel present. Those statements are, in my view, accurate and full statements. Yes, there will be more information, and those materials will be provided to the Defence. I used the three-week estimate based on your previous order that material -- any new material arising should be provided to the Defence three weeks before that material is brought up in court. I'm amenable to whatever the Court feels is appropriate on the timing of any new information from these accused. So yes, I agree there are some concerns with the changes in the indictment as -- that have been made more particular because of the input of the accused, and counsel should have some time, and I believe the Court is talking about time, and I would ask you to use your best judgement and we will of course abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be short on this one. Well, first, I believe the Prosecutor -- I don't want to say mischaracterised, but perhaps misunderstood my position. I would prefer not to go forward with Mr. Ruez. I'm prepared to the extent that I can, so I'm not in disagreement with the -- the Jokic Defence team. Number two: I must point out that with respect at least to Mr. Nikolic - I don't know about the Obrenovic situation - but with Mr. Nikolic, it would appear that there was a whole lot of shuttle diplomacy going on to agree to the negotiated facts. And I say "negotiated" because I don't have -- when we see that, it is not a statement where, for instance, a tape recorder was there, as the Rules would provide, and you punch that tape recorder and then you record all of the conversations. That's why I motioned for the handwritten notes. Also, depending on what I get from those notes, it may become necessary - and I say this with all due sincerity - it may become necessary for me to ask that everyone present during those negotiating sessions where the client -- the accused was there be subject to questioning, because in my opinion the client -- a client-attorney privilege no longer exists, they all have become witnesses, because we do not have an accurate recording -- a transparent recording from which everyone, the Defence, and more importantly the trial Bench can determine what exactly was said during those sessions. So it's not just the statements that I'm going to be following. And so that's why I made that motion. I made it on an expedited basis. I was told today that there might be a change in the Prosecution's position. They're typing the notes to the extent of what they think are not work product and I should be entitled to review. But I must -- I must stress this point, and I'm very, very concerned about what exactly, how many meetings took place, how many negotiated proffers were offered, at what point did they -- did Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Obrenovic agreed, "All right. I can live with these facts." You know, because -- and I think -- because I think that's what we're dealing with. And because of that, it complicated tremendously our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this -- to this line of speculation and complete misconstruction of what goes on in -- in a discussion with -- in the sort of agreement that went on here. This is -- it's highly inflammatory. It's wrong. It's painting a picture of a process that is a dignified and appropriate process, and I just -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but it's -- it's outrageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, what's your point on this very issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My point is, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry. My point, Your Honour, is this: Under the Rules, those meetings should have been tape recorded. We don't have that over here. I don't know exactly what transpired, how many meetings were held. And it complicates our situation. And that is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we have received your motion. We are considering it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I thought I would make some oral argument on behalf of my motion, since we're -- they're closely connected. But I don't want to take any additional time, Your Honour. But if we would have the month, I think it's a reasonable amount of time. The Prosecutor conceded that some time would -- would be needed for the Defence. I appreciate that gesture. And we've calculated it, and we believe a month would be fair for all parties concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You have to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of sentences. I will try and give you the arguments, the reasons why we believe that we should not continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Ruez in the light of the indictment that's about to be amended. And it's up to you, Your Honour, to decide whether this is relevant or not. In our transcript, in B/C/S, 46.10, 46.11, 46.12 have been amended from the words under the direction of Dragan Obrenovic and Dragan Jokic. They've been changed "Under the authority of Dragan Obrenovic and direction of Dragan Jokic." So we have prepared ourselves for the cross-examination. We wanted to ask Mr. Ruez who had questioned Dragan Jokic on the 14th of December regarding these circumstances, we wanted to ask how this procedure went and whether these amended arguments are a result of the interview that Dragan Jokic had given. That is why we fear that we are going to miss something that could be in our client's interest. That's our reserve, and that is why we're asking to assist us, so that we can prepare for this part of the cross-examination. We have no other intentions in this respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after hearing the two parties, we had a discussion on those matters. We must confess that the latest development concerning with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic has great impact to this case. So it's very reasonable for both parties to reassess their case, the present situation, the changes. So in principle we agree that we'll have a recess. As for how long the recess will be and when it will start, I think we need further consideration. We may inform you tomorrow. As for the present witness, we decided to continue the cross-examination of the present witness until we've finished with him because we have to attach some credibility to the testimony of this witness. If we let this witness go, still under the oath, for over a month, I think the whole testimony of this witness will be ruined and it would not be fair to the side of calling that witness. Of course, if we received the new indictment -- I mean, the amended indictment. If the Defence team found that there are some points they would like to ask this witness again, it is possible to call this witness back concerning of those new elements, if the Defence counsel show good cause. It is so decided. We'll call the witness and finish the cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like at this point -- I believe that you denied our motion to stay the proceedings completely at this point, and so I'd like to ask the Court to certify this decision for immediate appeal under Rule 73 and stay the proceedings at least for seven days until we can appeal this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as a normal practice, when we make decisions, I think if there's no other decisions from the Appeals Chamber or no other specific circumstances, we'll carry out that decision, and which you may file a written motion to appeal this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So is the President granting us certification to appeal or denying our request for certification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to make a decision at this moment. I hope you could file a written motion on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Could we stay the proceedings until we could get the written motion filed, if we do it within the next 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So we're proceeding. My concern is that the integrity of the proceedings are going to be in question if we're forced to proceed with the trial under the circumstances. And I know that this Trial Chamber wants a fair and a valid trial that's not subject to appeal at a later date. So one more time, I'm just going to stress that we object to proceeding at this moment and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I fail to see your point, because -- because I have already said that if you found the amended indictment is related to your client, you have the opportunity to call this witness back and question him on that particular point. I think that's fair enough. What's the reason for -- for appeal?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The reason for appeal is that it's fundamental error as far as the rights of the accused go to be informed about the charges against him under Article 20. To proceed at this point, it's fundamental error and violates the rights of the accused. And even by going forward and cross-examining a witness, although we will get a continuance afterwards, it's still proceeding with the trial, and I believe that there's fundamental error that's committed here that it affects the integrity of the proceedings at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in our view, that the indictment filed by the Prosecution on the 27th of May, 2002 is still valid. We will proceed based on this indictment. I don't see there is any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I will file a written motion for certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the witness, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I had hoped we had already finished that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: We had finished that discussion, Your Honour. And I'm going to go on to something that's not relevant to this witness, if you don't mind. We have not filed a written motion to suppress the interviews and interrogation of the accused from December 1999 and April 2000, and we will follow up with a written motion. But before we are going to cross-examine this witness, we would like under Rule 95, Article 18, Article 20, and Article 21 to allege that these statements were taken illegally and we will be challenging that. And so I wanted you to know ahead of time that we're objecting to the statements and we will file a written motion giving you our exact grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, are you ready to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before that, I have a few words to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, to the Defence team. If you are going to use any documents during your cross-examination which is not in the list of the Prosecution's binders or lists of the documents, you had better furnish us with a copy so that we could know what you are talking about. Another matter is: As a Defence counsel, you know, during the cross-examination, the witness is always hostile, you know. So I hope you could show patience, professionalism, and be polite to all the witnesses in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. And I hope that the remarks are not made as a result of some -- some of my earlier conduct in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course not. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ruez. It might be a little awkward given the way you're situated, so you may want to turn your chair a little bit. I take it you had a restful day yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, you know, just to set me at east, you didn't have any contact with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because rules are rules; right? And you have to follow the rules?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you're shaking your head. So we need to make a record.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, I want to talk with you a little bit about your background. But before we talk about your background in general, and since we're talking about rules, let me take you back to where we left off, the last item you talked about on direct examination. And let me refresh your memory. Towards the end of the direction examination, you were asked about participating in interviews of two of the accused; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You remember those interviews?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail for all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you remember being there during the interview.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond -- yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beyond a shadow of a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you've attended a lot of interviews.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that there is a particular procedure that you followed.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that because of your background as an experienced investigator or also because of the procedure that is set in the Rules -- you know, under the Rules here?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only because of the set of Rules which are -- which apply to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so I take it you were familiar with the Rules before you did the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to be familiar with them, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. And -- and if you were not familiar, you had all those lawyers with you. I mean, there were lawyers with you at the time working for the Office of the Prosecution, and so they could also assist you if you didn't know the Rules; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was indeed also part of the reason of their presence with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it, correct me if I'm wrong. I'm trying to visualise being there, I take it before you interviewed these witnesses you probably had a chat amongst yourselves to decide strategy, who would go first, you know, who would play the good guy or the bad guy, what topics would be divided among the individual questioners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I leave it to you to speculate on this, but there is part of truth in what you say, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'll leave out the good guy, bad guy routine, but you understand what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt, but just remember that you and the witness are speaking the same language, that is English. So the interpreters, you know, find it very difficult to follow you. So I will ask you to make a pause after the witness answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for reminding me of that. I -- I apologise to the translators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just so we walk through the procedure. Okay? Normally there would be a difference whether the individual was a witness or a suspect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the procedure would be if the person is deemed a suspect, you have to read him his rights.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those rights are right in the -- in the Rules, at least.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And they're very similar to what we see on television. You have the right to -- you know, to have a lawyer present, and anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law that, sort of stuff, basically. Right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't refer to American movies when I prepare my job, but you are probably a bit right as well, since some of these rules are coming from civil law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. In any event, there is a distinction when somebody is a suspect and somebody is a witness.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who would make that decision? Would that be you, or would that be somebody else, or would it be sort of a consensus among the team?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this topic, the way we are doing the things is quite simple. Me as the lead investigator of the case, I decide who are the people we should see in priority 1 and then those we should see then in maybe priority 2 or 3, but then the status that applies to them is decided by the person who at that time is called the legal advisor of the team and who then becomes the Prosecutor during the trials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So help me out here. Somebody could actually be a suspect; in other words, you suspect them of having participated and not just a mere witness, in other words, having information, but the team would decide whether to treat that individual as a suspect, where he would have the right to have a lawyer present, or as a witness, where he would not be advised of his rights.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we summon a person as a suspect, it is because not only we do suspect that he might be one but also because we already believe that we have hard evidence against him. If we do not have such hard evidence, though we might on a personal -- on our personal psychological ground believe that he might indeed be a suspect of something, if we do not have hard evidence against him, we will summon him probably as a -- as a witness, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that was the procedure that was followed throughout?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this is the procedure that we followed for all the -- all the persons that we interviewed through the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska, yes, all the Drina Corps officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, would there be a time during the interview, maybe because the witness was not as cooperative as you would like him or -- him to be, that you would inform him that you would turn him into a suspect?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall such a situation occurred, but it -- I don't recall. No, I cannot tell you. I would not say for sure this has never happened, because everything depends on how you present the thing. It might be -- it might look like a threat in the way you present it, but it can also be an advise for someone on which indeed you might not have hard evidence but you know that he could provide you some of it if he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I mean, the whole purpose is to squeeze the witness.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the whole purpose is to get truthful information from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so by informing him that you would turn him into a suspect when you brought him in as a witness without a lawyer, that is -- that is the approach that you would take.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I confirm I have no recollection this ever happened. It's just that under oath I cannot say for sure it never happened, because I cannot be a hundred per cent sure of this. But I have no recollection it ever happened with any of the people we ever interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I'm not accusing you, by the way, of you ever doing that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your point. No worry. I'm just trying to answer honestly to your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Good. And that's all I'm asking. That's all I'm asking. Now, I take it when somebody would come, you would tape record that statement?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you first, before you would begin the questioning process, did you first maybe have a chat with him to sort of negotiate what sort of facts he might agree to before you would start the questioning process?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only question we asked prior starting the tape was inviting the person to have a coffee at the bar of the -- the Banja Luka facility where we were. But we never talked about the content of what we would discuss before starting the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the coffee was to kind of relax you. Have a coffee, have a cigarette, relax, and then when the -- when the formal questioning would begin, it would be on tape.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Politeness first, and job second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And during -- when he would have that coffee, by the way, you weren't talking about the incident that he might -- that you might be questioning him about or the information that you might want to get from him.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in his presence, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wouldn't be asking him, "Well, if you could agree to certain facts in advance, so then when you would go on tape later on, you could frame your questions in a way that you would elicit the facts that you had agreed on during the coffee session?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm curious to know what you would come up with, because I know we would not do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all, let me assure you, these are not trick questions. And I am not trying to suggest that that was the method in which you conducted the investigation -- these questionings.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, feel free. I'm here to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the procedure would be the witness, or if he was a suspect, would come to Banja Luka, step one.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You would invite him at a particular time and -- and date; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would offer him some coffee.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would make the offer, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And then when the questioning began, it would be done so with a tape recorder tape recording every single word that was spoken.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Now I see the point. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you'll be able to share it with us at some point too, but for right now I would appreciate it if you would just follow along with me. Now, when there would -- when there were breaks, as you indicated, the witness might want a break, you and your colleagues might want a break. There was a particular procedure that was followed as well. Right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that procedure was to notify that you're going on break on tape, with the exact time.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'd have your break.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the break, when you went back on tape, you would again notify -- note on the tape what time it was, and you might even ask the witness or the suspect whether anything was talked about during the break.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the whole purpose for having that procedure in place is to make sure that we have some sort of a transparent record from which all of us who were not there at the time could later on figure out and know what exactly happened; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under any normal circumstances, yes, indeed this is what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It protects you as the questioner.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So lawyers like myself would never, you know, try to suggest that something was said when in fact it wasn't, because we have a tape recorded statement that is also going to -- will get transcribed later on; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, if it's ever challenged by the witness as to what he had said, you have his voice and you can say, "Here. Read about it. Hear about it." Right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, if there's ever a question with respect to the translation -- because after all, you're speaking English. There's a translator. It's being spoken in a language which you may not understand. You're going to get the answer in another language. Then it's going to be translated to you. This way we can verify to make sure that everything was done by the number. So everyone, you, the witness, the lawyers, the Court, would know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One last question on that area: Would it be fair to say that that was the procedure that was set in place?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to the next segment of my -- my direct -- of my cross-examination. Let's talk a little bit about -- when did you arrive at the -- when did you begin working as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working as a police superintendent in judicial police in France in 1987.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, and whereabouts in France was that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Paris.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the big city, where everything -- lots of resources. Everything done is in a very specific manner.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before becoming an inspector with the judicial police, I take it you -- one had to go to the police academy; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not an inspector. I was a superintendent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A superintendent. Okay. Well, tell us, how did you become a superintendent?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In France, there are several ways to become a superintendent. In the police, the way I -- I took was after my law studies, I passed a competition that enabled me to enter the national superior school of police, and at the end of two years of that school you have the rank of a superintendent in France. You don't need to become first an inspector and go through the ranks. So indeed, I'm not a crime scene technician, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, I was going to ask that question, but thank you for volunteering it. Okay. Now, if I have -- and since you're working with the judicial police, I take it that you are dedicated to a particular area.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is a national police. I later worked in Marseilles and also in Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but what I meant -- and I apologise for phrasing the question inartfully. You were dedicated to the judicial police department?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, that's the department that does all the investigations for the Prosecution and for the -- the investigative judges?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So at -- at some point during a particular case, are they both your bosses?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it that when you are in France working as a superintendent in the judicial police, when the case begins you are under the -- the direction of the prosecution to some extent; right? A crime happens; something needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. The system is very different than in the US.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand the system. I know your system somewhat, not adds good -- well as you do. But at some point the case may go to the investigative judge; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. He's the independent judge. He stands between the prosecute and the trial judge; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, he is the one that will be doing the formal questioning of witnesses and suspects; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, is that question relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It will become relevant at some point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please be soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for reminding me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is they who directed the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On paper, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you came -- and how long did you work in that position?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight years in the capacity of superintendent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say you joined. Were you seconded from France, or did you quit your job and become a regular employee of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation is in the middle of two, in fact, I was not seconded. I was an employee of the United Nations, but at the time the Tribunal made a request to France to provide personnel, so there was the first selection among these candidates, and then an ultimate selection done by the ICTY. So I was detached, not seconded, detached, but I was paid by the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so you were on the payroll of -- of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were under the direction of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you say ICTY, does that mean in general the Tribunal or does that mean a particular segment, the Registry, OTP, Defence?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigation section of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you were a -- you were a member of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that you were the chief investigator for Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were in charge of the investigation, or does that -- meaning that you would direct how the investigation would go, or that you were just the top investigator among a team of investigators in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several stages during this investigation, but at the very early stages I was the only one working on this. There was no team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you're the only one, you can always be the chief, right, because there's nobody behind you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, since you were the first one, as others followed, and since you had the institutional memory of the case, and of course on your skills and professionalism, you advanced to be the chief investigator.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't happen like this. At the early stages, as I told you, there was no team. And some colleagues would go and assist me on the basis of the possibilities that they have to leave their own activities. And after the missions they were returning to their teams and I was continuing with the topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who was your boss for this investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of investigations at that time was named Cees Hendricks at the early stages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so it is he who would give you your assignments?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was proposing what to do, and I was not prevented to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was he also attached to the -- part of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the investigation section at the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in -- okay. At the early stages, then, it is the investigators that are out there investigating Srebrenica and not the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we are -- I'm waiting for the translation. We are all members of the Office of the Prosecutor. All the people who went with me on field missions were members of the Office of the Prosecutor. They were not just -- they were just not people who were under my command, if one can say so, since they were attached to other teams. It was not a structured team. A team was created early 1997 to deal with this subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any Prosecutors also assigned to be part of this -- this process?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Prosecutor who joined this case was Mr. McCloskey, who joined me at the end of 1996, and this is -- he was the second permanent member of this team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that capacity, what was his position? I mean, since he joined the team, what was he there for?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- he was working with me, but we were not a structure. When it became a structure, so early 1997, the title of Mr. McCloskey was legal adviser. There was always an legal adviser attached to an investigation team leader. So Mr. McCloskey became this legal advisor early 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was advising you. So am I fair to assume or conclude that you were in charge and Mr. McCloskey was there to provide you with legal advice and to assist in other ways?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were doing everything together. Making all decisions together, even digging in mass graves together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in charge is the team leader of the investigation at that time. It was then later the situation changed after I left the Tribunal, but at that time the head of the investigations was the investigation team leader and he was assisted by the Prosecutor who had the name of legal adviser.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge then? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jean-Rene Ruez. I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you and. And so you directed the investigations, how it would go?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who you would select to interview?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we couldn't select all those we were willing to interview, we had to do indeed such a selection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where the investigation would start?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that point. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let me walk you back. Sometime in July 1995 you were assigned to the Srebrenica investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was initially requested to go to the field and check the -- I mean, how serious the press information was, the press information that came out immediately at that time was about massacres, but there was still no evidence that any massacre had really been committed, and this is why I was sent first, as a kind of assessment mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time, as I recall, before you were sent, you were already in Tuzla at that point?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I left The Hague, and reached Tuzla via Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you made your first trip back in -- in July 1995 in the field.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was my first mission for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you by yourself, or were there others?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was accompanied by Ms. Stephanie Frease, who was also working for the Office of the Prosecutor at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was she doing?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was an analyst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you had a language assistant, or does she speak Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: She also speaks Serbo-Croatian, and we had also one language assistant, Ms. Adis Karamuratovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point, were you asked -- when you became the leader of this team, was it you that designed how this case would progress in the investigations phase?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation was already running since one and a half years, once the -- before the team was created, so at that time it was a natural flow of decisions that had to be made, since there were very clear phases to be conducted in this investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, prior to the formal team structure, who was the person that sat down and mapped out how this case would be investigated? What -- you know, where the start would be, whether it would be just go to the field, collect evidence, assemble a team, visit the various brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was making proposals on a written mission plans, and these mission plans were accepted by the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the chain of command, that would be your boss.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the missions were assigned by the chief of investigations, who was John Ralston, after Mr. Cees Hendricks left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said written proposals, so there's -- there's some documentation as to what you proposed, you know, and how you proposed the investigations should progress.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the first step that you proposed - do you recall - the first step to be done in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was to scan among the -- the initial information obtained by the local Bosniak police as well as the war crime commission, select among a large group of witnesses those we had to interview in priority in order to begin to draft a raw picture of the events and the various areas in which we needed to investigate, one part being the situation in Potocari, the other one the situation in the woods, the other one the situation along the road between Srebrenica and Kladanj, and the fourth main group, all what is mass killings, and that got indeed our attention as a priority 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so that -- that had priority before even visiting, for instance, the brigade headquarters to seize documents.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Reconstruction of the facts is indeed something indispensable before trying to find out who committed these facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But would it be fair to say - and correct me if I'm wrong - that fairly early on in the investigation it was -- you began to have some suspicions from your years as -- as a superintendent as to who might be involved, you know, which brigades might have been involved or civilian authorities might have been involved in the atrocities?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At what point did you make the decision to -- to go to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the possibility was there. In reality, what happened at that time was that we intended to conduct the search, since already such a long time. We didn't have both the manpower to do it by ourselves, nor exactly the timing due to a lot of other aspects of the case we needed to deal with. So in fact, we used the opportunity of a search that was getting prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor in another area of Republika Srpska and enlarge this mission in order to be able to use that manpower put in place for one circumstance, to use it to do three headquarters, so not only the 5th Corps was done but for the sake of another case, but also the Zvornik Brigade search could be done and the Bratunac Brigade search could be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My question was when? Before you gave us that lengthy narration which didn't answer my question. So if you could tell us when, I would appreciate it, and then we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to please you by giving these details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I am pleased. I am pleased. But let me do my job too. Let me ask the questions, and you can give me the answers.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to answer by yes or no, I can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you -- I asked a when question, when. You can give me the date, if you recall. If you don't recall, you can refer to some notes.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to recall. Give me just two seconds. That was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you get on the job to start the investigation in 1995 in July, and it's in 1998 that you pay your first visit to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters along with the other areas that you were going to search; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in fact in -- I'm waiting for translation. To be very precise, we did pay a visit, as you say it, to the Bratunac Brigade - that was in June 1996 - in order to search and seize equipment that had been taken from the UN battalion that was stored in a container just in front of the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade. These were flak jackets, as well as blue helmets that had been repainted in grey colour in order to be later used by Bratunac Brigade people after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's an assumption that you're make; right? The paint -- the use of the paint --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not an assumption. Talking about it with an assistant of Mr. Blagojevic, he said that that equipment was designed to be used for de-miners, who could not have such quality equipment to fulfil their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you were there in 1996 in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to seize - that was the word that you used; am I correct - to seize UN equipment?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To seize UN equipment in possession of the RS military unit

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But you were there to seize equipment?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So this almost what -- in what year -- what month are we talking about in 1996?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely, but it was in the middle of the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since you were there to seize UN equipment and you were there on an investigation and you already had by this point nine or ten years' experience as an investigator, did you ever think that it might be a good idea to seize documents or to go and try to find out what, if anything else, might be there at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters? After all, you were there. No sense in making another trip, costing all the donor's extra money for you to go there. Why not say, " By the way, since I'm here, I want to collect all the documents you might have just in case later on they might disappear."

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have loved doing that as early as we could access RS territory, but during that mission my backpack was not big enough to vacuum-clean the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I come from Alaska, and they tell us whenever you go out to the woods, you've got to take your ten essentials because you never know what might happen when you're out. The question is: Since you were going there, as an investigator, would it not be sensible to take the necessary precautions just in case you found all these documents, so you could have them, analyse them, or others to analyse?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a step that unfortunately, due to the way we were organised at the time, we couldn't do before the date we did it. But indeed, I totally agree with you, had we even been able to do that in summer 1995, I would have had pleasure to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Naturally -- naturally, if I were to look through your requisitions or your proposals, I would find something in there, in those documents - I don't know if they have been disclosed to us, but I certainly will be making that request, to see every -- all your proposals - but naturally, I would find something there, a piece of paper, with your signature, making the request, either before or after at least - definitely after - to go back to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to get documents. I would find some kind of a request from you; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you would not find that, because during the year 1996, for example, our top priority was based on the information received from the approximately ten survivors of mass executions that we had already talked with, our top priority in 1996 was to identify these crime scenes and start exhumations. We were not in 1996 in any way in a position to start conducting searches in military units. We did not need -- we did not even at that time know if our crime bases was a serious one or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, did you ever make the request; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 1998 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1996, after you went to the Bratunac Brigade, did you make the request; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you make a request for resources, yes or no, for that particular mission?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My request for resources was a bit of the same of your objections that, are continuous -- continuous requests I was making, continuous requests during 1995 and 1996 and 1997 to get additional resources, that I got once John Ralston became chief of investigations, not before he became chief of investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was rather specific: Did you make a specific request in writing or even orally for more resources so you could go back to the Bratunac Brigade to get the documents? Because after all, you were able to go there and retrieve helmets.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely not the same type of operation. When you are on a mission, in theatre, to retrieve a bunch of helmets from a container than to organise a search mission in a brigade headquarter. And I repeat my answer to your precise question: No, I did not make such a request at that time. It was out of our range at that time to start doing searches in military facilities in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- now, when you say "our range," meaning the -- the Office of the Prosecution range?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a case where, according to the Prosecution, is the largest atrocity in Western Europe since the holocaust?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I share your astonishment, and unfortunately I have to answer yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they had resources to send you to collect helmets, and they had to foresight to send you to collect helmets but not documents.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been sent to take helmets. It occurred that during that mission I had a talk with an American soldier who told me that he had seen this equipment in that container. So through the liaison officer, who was Major Golic at that time, the liaison officer of the Drina Corps with the American Brigade, I made the request to get access to these helmets and check what they were. And this is what we did. And when we realised it was equipment that was belonging to DutchBat, I seized them in order to check who they had been taken from and in what circumstances they had been taken from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you've finished that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take the break right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, before we left off, we were speaking about your visit at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. We're still there, by the way, back in 1996. You were there to, you indicated, to collect some items that belonged to the UN. On that particular visit, did you happen to see Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't there when you first got there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there, I think -- no, only on one occasion, because before I went there, it was an oral request to Major Golic, and that we gave him more or less a week to fulfil the demand, and that was not done the day I was supposed to leave the mission area. So then we went together with the American major, who was our security guarantee in the area, and he made so to enforce my request to get access to this material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- let me rephrase the question. I -- I wasn't clear, so I apologise. Okay. When you went there with the American major, when you got to the brigade headquarters, was Mr. Blagojevic there or did he show up shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who was there was the Lieutenant Lazar Ostojic and to Colonel Blagojevic arrived a bit later dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is: Yes, he showed up afterwards, after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now that you ask if he arrived after, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, did you manage to collect the items that you were there to collect?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you recognise, by the way, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He changed a bit, but I do recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise him at the time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we didn't know who the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was in July 1995. We had option among two possible names. So I did request Mr. Blagojevic -- Colonel Blagojevic, I asked him only two questions. One was what he knew about the origin and the use of the equipment. He did not answer. He asked me a second question. The second question was: Since when are you the commander of the Bratunac Brigade? I did receive no answer, and got lectured on the fact that the calibre of the weapons used by the American forces, 5.56, were against the Geneva Conventions. But he never answered my question about who he was and since when he was in that capacity commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me go back to my questions, and maybe you could answer my questions. When you saw Mr. Blagojevic, did you recognise him to be Mr. Blagojevic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen that man before that day, and I couldn't recognise him since I didn't even know who he was, aside that he was presented as being the commander that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is no, you did not recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not recognise someone who I didn't know before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it your testimony today that in 1996 you had never heard of Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew about two possible names as being head of that brigade in summer 1995. One of these I don't remember today, and the second one was Colonel Blagojevic, but we had no certainty about who was who really in summer 1995. And Colonel Blagojevic did not answer that question when I asked that to him in June 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So the answer is back in 1996, when you went there, you had heard of a Colonel Blagojevic who at one point, sometime in 1995 in July, at one point or another, or thereafter or slightly before, was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat again: In 1995, the information I got probably at that time both from Bosniak police or contacts with the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army at that time, I asked if they had any information about who was the -- what was the name of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade in 1995. They did not know for sure. I could not get a certainty answer. I was provided with two names. One of these names was Colonel Blagojevic, but I didn't know even in June 1996 if indeed it was Colonel Blagojevic who had been the brigade commander in 1995. I did not know that in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you had that information in your memory when you were there in 1996 at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. That information that you just told us.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That optionally he could have been the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you -- did you ever -- at that point, did you try to get a photograph of Mr. Blagojevic to see what he looked like so just in case you ran into him, you could ask him some questions?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The circumstances at the time were such that the main priority in that area for the people who were assisting us was to create a positive relationship with the VRS armed forces. Had I started taking pictures of all the people from the VRS side we came in -- we came across at that time, I would have jeopardised that relationship. So indeed, I did not take a photograph of Colonel Blagojevic at that time, since I had no certainty about who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe -- maybe it's the translation. My question was: Did you have a photograph of him? In other words, when you started doing your investigation, as a good investigator and you would hear these names, you would begin to see if there were photographs someplace so you could put photograph, name, and then if the opportunity ever arose and you came up to that person, you could say, "Ah, this must be Obrenovic, this must be Jokic, this must be Blagojevic. Might I try to get information from them?" Did you do that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people I was in contact with didn't have any photograph of Mr. Blagojevic available at that time when I asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the time that you were there in 1996, during that session - and I take it you were at the headquarters for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did Mr. Blagojevic ever have -- speak with the major? Did they talk at all?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I recall, they might have even had a rakija together?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all had rakija together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, that's the local home brew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And in the regulations of the US for those who are in contact with the VRS armed forces they are exceptionally allowed to have a little sip of alcohol with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Because US servicemen, especially officers, are not supposed to be drinking in uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true for the army personnel, not necessarily for an investigator of the ICTY in specific circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't mentioning you. I was just worried about the major, so we don't get him in trouble. So all of you, you, the major, Mr. Blagojevic, sat down, comfortable during that two-hour period, had rakija and waited until the business of -- of taking those -- that UN property was finished; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
